newsitem.title: TAIWAN: S.Koreans start anti-nuke hunger strike in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: S.Koreans start anti-nuke hunger strike in Taiwan.

text.p: Six South Korean anti-nuclear activists began a planned five-day hunger strike in Taipei on Wednesday to pressure Taiwan to cancel a controversial deal to ship nuclear waste to Stalinist North Korea.

The activists from Green Korea, an independent environment group in South Korea, and local anti-nuclear groups had minor clashes with Taiwan Power Co workers when the protesters tried to take their complaints into the state utility's headquarters.
"Rad waste -- Don't export. Don't make," read a banner held by the South Korean activists.

Under a January 11 contract, Taipower can ship up to 200,000 barrels of nuclear waste to impoverished and food-strapped North Korea. Unconfirmed media reports have said Taipower will pay North Korea US$1,150 per barrel.
"The Taiwan government is trying to solve its mounting waste problem by profiting from the serious famine in North Korea," Green Korea leader Jang Won said in a prepared statement.

"For people seeking environmental justice, such exports are an immoral form of environmental terrorism that endanger not only the population of North Korea, but that of the entire northeast Asian region," Jang said.
Jang shaved his head in protest and said his group was starting a five-day hunger strike.

Taipower workers, saying South Korea had no right to interfere in what they called a legitimate business deal between Taipei and Pyongyang, blockaded Taipower's entrance and shouted: "Go back" and "Koreans get out."
"If they want to protest, they should have protested in their own country. They should not have come to Taipower," Yao Chiang-lin, Taipower's union chairman, told reporters.
"We can't be bullied easily," another Taipower worker said.
Despite the escalating protests, Taiwan and North Korea forged ahead on Tuesday with preparations for an initial shipment of 60,000 barrels of low-level nuclear waste.
South Korea, worried the deal could pollute the Korean peninsula with radioactivity, says there is no verification that the North -- Seoul's arch-rival -- can store the waste safely.
Taiwan maintains the Taipei-Pyongyang waste pact complies with all international regulations and that shipments would be securely packed in steel barrels.

North Korea's Soviet-inspired heavy-water nuclear programme caused international uproar in the early 1990s, with Washington, Seoul and other Pacific countries alleging it aimed to develop nuclear weapons.
A key concern was a lack of international supervision.
Under intense pressure, Pyongyang agreed in 1994 to freeze and eventually junk the nuclear programme in exchange for US$4.5 billion in safer nuclear technology and interim power.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with either North Korea or South Korea, both of which recognise Taiwan's own rival -- the communist Chinese government in Beijing.
